title: Interstate banking deregulation on credit supply

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
We will use a Difference-in-Differences (DID) approach to estimate the causal effect of interstate banking deregulation on credit supply. The DID method is appropriate here because we have a treatment group (states that deregulated) and a control group (states that did not deregulate), and we can compare the changes in credit supply before and after deregulation between these groups.

The key assumption in DID is parallel trends, which means that in the absence of deregulation, the credit supply in treated and control states would have followed the same trend over time. We will check this assumption graphically and statistically.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(plm)
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# Read the data
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s05_data.csv")

# Convert the data to a panel data frame
pdata <- pdata.frame(data, index = c("unit_id", "period"))

# Estimate the DID model
did_model <- plm(y ~ post + treat_x_post, data = pdata, model = "within")

# Print the coefficient for the treatment effect
summary(did_model)$coefficients["treat_x_post", "Estimate"]

# Robustness check: Clustered standard errors
coeftest(did_model, vcovHC(did_model, type = "HC1"))

# Check for parallel trends (graphical)
# Create a balanced panel for the first 4 periods
pdata_balanced <- subset(pdata, period <= 4)

# Estimate the model for the balanced panel
balance_model <- plm(y ~ post, data = pdata_balanced, model = "within")

# Plot the coefficients
plot(coeftest(balance_model, vcovHC(balance_model, type = "HC1")), xlab = "Period", ylab = "Coefficient", main = "Parallel Trends Check")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
```

## 3. Expected Findings
We expect the coefficient on the `treat_x_post` variable to be positive, indicating that interstate banking deregulation increased credit supply in deregulated states compared to regulated states. The magnitude of the effect will depend on the data, but we expect it to be economically significant given the potential for increased competition and efficiency in the banking sector following deregulation. The parallel trends assumption should hold if there is no systematic difference in the pre-deregulation trends between treated and control states. If the assumption holds, the DID estimate will provide a credible estimate of the causal effect of interstate banking deregulation on credit supply.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: DID — treated=deregulated states, control=still-regulated; shock=deregulation date
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Credit supply increases significantly after deregulation
